title: I Was Wrong About ChatGPT and AI (Part 1 of 3)
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: In the first of a three-part series, Stuart walks back his earlier dismissal of ChatGPT ("ain't no thing but a chicken wing"), explaining that conversations with fellow teacher-writers Jim Burke and Matthew Johnson, plus three months of his own hands-on use, changed his view of the technology's significance for teaching. He catalogs a long list of personal experiments — asking ChatGPT for relationship advice, outing ideas for his kids, tweet-generation, interview-question brainstorming, discussion questions for Things Fall Apart, and explanations of the Atlantic Revolutions pitched at a 12-year-old's level — framing the tool alternately as an "intelligent search engine" and a "lackey." He's careful to flag its failure mode too: when asked about "Dave Stuart Jr.," ChatGPT confidently invented a book he never wrote, which he uses as a concrete illustration of AI hallucination and misinformation risk. The piece previews Parts 2 and 3, promising to explain what he thinks AI will and won't change about teaching, and closes by reassuring readers that even in an AI-saturated future, teaching remains one of the most rewarding careers available.
points: Stuart's reversal is anchored in specific, replicable use cases (relationship advice, lesson-question brainstorming, translating a complex history topic for a 12-year-old) rather than abstract hype, giving teacher-readers testable examples of ChatGPT's capability.

The hallucination episode — ChatGPT insisting Stuart wrote a nonexistent book, twice, even after being asked to double-check — is offered as firsthand evidence for why AI misinformation concerns are legitimate, not paranoid.
He frames ChatGPT's value along two axes — "intelligent search engine" and "lackey" — a simple heuristic for what kinds of tasks the tool is actually useful for.
Despite the reversal, Stuart explicitly signals he isn't converting to "tech-ification of learning," setting up the more skeptical, pedagogy-first argument he develops in Parts 2 and 3.
quotes: Just three months ago, I wrote an article about how ChatGPT "ain't no thing but a chicken wing.

It was this idea that ChatGPT represented a new source of teacher demoralization that struck me during that conversation. My "chicken wing" article was trying to vaguely remedy this, I think, but I realized that I hadn't taken the matter as earnestly as it deserved.

In short, I began using chatbots as something like a multitalented assistant. With much greater ease and clarity than a Google search, it helped me brainstorm teaching prompts, manage relational struggles, overcome inner blocks, and generate fun ideas for outings with my kids.
It wasn't all puppies and rainbows. Once, the machine tried to gaslight me into thinking I had written a book that I've never written.
So, if you've heard folks saying that they're worried about this technology spreading misinformation, this is part of where that concern comes from.

And, just so you don't have to worry, let me spoil the ending: even if this goes where I think it's going, teaching is still going to be one of the most rewarding and entertaining and delightful ways to spend one's career.
